items.title: Earl Turbinton Interview, 1990-09-01
items.q: i was learning fast uh and being tutored by john o'neill who had had some success with the free southern theater

ctx.x: we're getting a a wide spectrum of people all kind of uh we're getting a a wide range of uh people interested in the workshop um in addition to the support of people uh interested like louberglade and uh jules khan and and their friends and other persons that were like patrons of the arts and sense and connoisseurs of jazz that were more familiar with uh the traditional jazz but they saw that what we were trying to do with the newer music was very logical and an extension of like the kind of things that had been…

the things that were money generating things that would have kept the place afloat and but it was a very warm and i'll never forget the loving uh atmosphere that was there and how these various cross sections of people came together uh another thing that's very that was uh very interesting that happened as a result of the workshop is that one of the groups of people that understood what we were going through possibly as much or more than anybody else was john o'neill and the people at the free southern theater…

which was half of the group at that time. And it was a long time. I mean, many, many years before I ever played with anybody that gave me the completeness and the fullness of playing with that particular group. In fact, we've never ever had that same setting together again. There have been times when it's been George French, David Lee, Willie T, and myself, or Willie T, David Lee, myself, or Willie T, Joyce Davis, and myself, but not all four of us back together again.
